sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present the Prior-Fitted Language Model (PFLM), a 300M-parameter byte-level transformer pretrained only on samples from a synthetic non-linguistic prior. Given a prefix of real text, it learns to predict the language in context with frozen weights, having never seen a word of any real language. Every training sequence is generated by a recurrent structural causal model drawn fresh from a distribution over such models. The model never sees the same language twice during training, so the only way to predict the continuation is to infer the language from the prefix. Samples from this prior share the statistical signatures of natural text: Zipfian frequencies, slow entropy-rate convergence, and long-range dependence. On Wikipedia in six languages, bits per byte fall from the uniform eight to between 0.9 and 2.4 at one million bytes of context. Given numerals instead of text, PFLM learns to count, to compare magnitudes, and to add approximately. It predicts deterministic sequences like Rudin-Shapiro or the prime indicator, and it compresses six non-text domains, from source code to speech, below gzip and PPMd. The model has not learned a language. It has learned to learn one.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: What evolution gives child is not language but the ability to acquire one. After tens of millions of words, child is fluent in whichever language surrounds them. modern language model is trained on tens of trillions. This six-order-of-magnitude gap is not fact about language. It is fact about how much prior knowledge each brings to the data. The childs prior is not knowledge of any specific language but expectations about what any language can be: wide enough to admit any of them, narrow enough to learn one. Human languages occupy bounded region in the space of possible symbol systems, and the childs hypothesis space is that region. language model begins with no such prior. Its inductive biases are architectural: generic pressures toward smoothness and compositionality that say nothing about what language can be. Every regularity it learns about language must be inferred from the corpus alone. This is why models lag at inferences humans do effortlessly. baby learns whichever language surrounds them from the speech they hear. child, born with sense of quantity, gradually learns to count, compare, and do arithmetic. mathematician recognizes the rule producing an unfamiliar sequence from its first terms. Each rests on prior knowledge of what languages, what numbers, or what sequences can be: evolution and experience supply the structure on which finite evidence rests. The model has neither, and must extract from trillions of tokens what humans inherit or learn. The asymmetry suggests recipe. Equip the model with prior, not over one language but over the family of possible languages. Sample fresh language for every pretraining sequence; the model never sees the same one twice. It cannot memorize any specific language, only learn to acquire one from prefix. The pretraining task is meta-learning by construction. The trained network performs amortized Bayesian inference over the prior. Prior-Fitted Networks [16, 25] establish the recipe on tabular classification and regression, since extended to various settings such as in-context regression of function classes [11], survival analysis [32], and algorithmic sequences from random programs [13]. We carry it to language: prior over synthetic languages (where we use the term language to indicate the domain of structured sequences) whose samples pre-train transformer, the Prior-Fitted Language Model (PFLM).1 To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has shown language model learning to predict natural language in context after pretraining only on samples from constructed non-linguistic prior. Every language model to date, however synthetic its curriculum, has been trained on natural language [10, 14, 22]. Our prior is recurrent structural causal model (SCM). One independently sampled SCM defines one synthetic language. The SCM evolves latent state through random graph of structural equations, emitting one token per step. Each token depends, by construction, on the tokens before it. The priors samples reproduce the signature statistics of natural text: Zipfian token frequencies, slow entropy-rate convergence, mutual-information decay at multiple scales. The prior is constructed, not fit; its samples occupy the same statistical neighborhood as natural text without sharing any specific script. byte-level transformer trained on samples from this prior infers natural language in context. Its training data contains no natural-language text. On every language we evaluate, bits per byte falls steadily with increasing context (Figure 1), from the uniform rate of eight to between 0.9 and 2.4 at one million bytes. Given numerals in context, the same model learns to count, to compare quantities, and to add approximately, the pattern of number sense seen in children before they can calculate [2, 7]. Beyond language and number, the model predicts deterministic sequences like RudinShapiro [1], Kolakoski [37], or the prime indicator, where each term follows from generating rule rather than frequency.

sections.title: 2 The Synthetic-Language Prior
sections.content: PFLM is trained on synthetic data alone: every pretraining sequence is sample from prior π over synthetic languages. This section instantiates the idea (Section 2.1), builds the prior (Sections 2.2 and 2.3), and specifies the model that approximates the predictor it induces (Section 2.4). 2.1 In-context inference over languages fresh language generates every training sequence, and the model sees only the resulting tokens, never the language that produced them. The only way to drive down next-token loss is to infer the generating language from the prefix. Next-token prediction is thus Bayesian inference [39]. The difficulty of prediction lives in the emitted sequence of discrete tokens. The latent state is first-order Markov: given ht, the past is irrelevant. The observed process is not. Each token yt quantizes the first dobs coordinates and discards the rest, lossy view of the Markov chain. The unobserved coordinates act as hidden memory, so the optimal predictor of yt+1 is filter, maintaining posterior over ht given the full prefix. 2.3 The prior over languages We sample ℓ π by drawing each component of the tuple independently. The graph is built node by node: each node receives parent set whose size is sampled uniformly from per-language range, with members drawn without replacement from {1, . . . , d}. Each structural equation fi is drawn per node from one of six functional families  (Table 1)  , with coefficients from Gaussians whose widths are sampled per language. Each activation σi is drawn from {tanh, softsign, clip, sin, id}, the noise scale η from fixed range, and the depth from per-language range. Each ρi is periodic: node updates at the steps with ϕi (mod ri) and skips the others. The rate ri {1, 2, 4, . . .} is drawn from geometric-style distribution over powers of two, biased so most nodes fire every step and small tail updates every 2, 4, 8, or more. The phase ϕi is drawn uniformly from {0, . . . , ri 1}, which de-synchronizes nodes with the same rate. The hyperparameter ranges are listed in Section A. To produce one pretraining sequence we draw language ℓ π, initialize h0 [1, 1]d, roll the dynamics in Equation (2) forward for steps, and emit the token stream (y1, . . . , yT ) via Equation (3), one token per step as drawn in Figure 2(b). The initialization law is itself sampled per sequence from six families on [1, 1]: uniform on sub-interval, Gaussian, Beta, two-point near 1, bimodal, and sparse, with most coordinates exactly zero. 2.4 Model and training PFLM is 300M-parameter decoder-only transformer  (Table 4)  trained by next-token prediction to approximate the posterior predictive of Equation (1). The model is hybrid stack similar to Qwen3-Next [40]: gated linear-attention layers [42] interleaved with attention layers in 3:1 ratio, the attention restricted to sliding window of 218 tokens. The linear-attention layers run in linear time and carry recurrent state across the sequence, while the sliding-window attention layers add exact recall within that window, so the stack is sub-quadratic and trains on sequences far longer than full attention permits. 5 Learning to Learn Language PREPRINT Table 1: The six structural-equation families. sections.title: 3 Statistical Signatures of the Prior
sections.content: Samples from the SCM prior match natural language across its statistical signatures, from byte marginals to long-range dependencies. We test against four data-free comparators whose parameters are sampled rather than fitted on text: i.i.d. uniform, i.i.d. Zipf, random bigram, and random hidden Markov model (HMM). The natural-language sources are English, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Japanese, and Korean Wikipedia, each contributing 500 sequences of 4096 bytes. The prior is sampled here at the configuration of the family that best matches these statistics. The training configuration (Section A) is instead chosen on transfer to natural language. 3.1 Scalar fingerprints Each baseline fails differently. The i.i.d. uniform, bigram, and HMM baselines produce near-uniform marginal distributions: byte entropy at the log2 256 = 8-bit ceiling, gzip ratio near one, all 256 bytes active. The i.i.d. Zipf baseline fixes the marginal [29, 44] but lacks conditional structure between adjacent bytes, missing the natural-language cluster on compression and Zipf exponent. Only the SCM prior lies in the natural-language band on all four statistics. 6 Learning to Learn Language PREPRINT (a) Entropy rate convergence. (b) Mutual information decay. Figure 4: The SCM prior reproduces both the slow entropy-rate convergence and the slow long-range MI decay of natural language. Synth shows the median (line) and 1090 percentile range (band) across 500 SCM samples; each natural language is the per-sequence median across 500 wiki sequences. (a) Conditional entropy H(Yt Yt1, . . . , Ytn+1) at n-gram orders 18. The synth band covers every natural-language curve at every order; dotted reference at = log2 256 = 8 bits is the i.i.d. uniform-random ceiling. (b) MI(Yt; Yt+d) at log-spaced distances = 1, 2, 4, . . . , 512 bytes. Synth and natural decay together from = 1 to = 512 bytes. 3.2 Trajectory statistics Natural languages converge their entropy rate slowly [4, 34]: each successive order of context strips less than bit from the conditional entropy (Figure 4a). This reflects weak but persistent dependencies at every scale. The SCM prior produces the same trajectory: its median tracks the natural-language band from 5 bits at = 1 down to under one bit at = 8. The 1090 envelope contains every natural-language curve. Long-range structure is the most discriminating signature [8, 9] (Figure 4b). Natural-language MI decays slowly without dropping to zero, from 2 bits at = 1 to 0.10.5 bits at = 512 [20]. The SCM priors median follows the same shape, and its 1090 envelope brackets every natural-language curve. This long-range MI traces specifically to the multi-rate firing schedule. An ablation that fixes ρi 1 for every node leaves the scalar fingerprints unchanged but reduces the priors long-range mutual information, integrated over distance, by 18%; the tail of slow nodes is what carries dependencies across many steps. 4 In-Context Learning on Real Data Every result in this section is produced from single model, trained only on samples from the synthetic prior of Section 2. We report bits per byte (BPB) for the byte streams, accuracy for the number tasks, and bits per symbol for the digit sequences (each over binary alphabet, so chance is one bit). Section gives the corpora and protocol. 4.1 Natural language On six languages, the model lowers its cost as the context grows, from the uniform rate of eight bits to between 0.9 and 2.4 bits at one million bytes (Figure 1a). Each curve conditions the model on growing prefix of Wikipedia, in English, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Japanese, and Korean, and measures bits per byte at each position. The curves differ in level for two reasons. Under UTF-8 character costs one byte in the Latin script, two in Arabic, and three in Devanagari and in the Chinese, Japanese, and Korean scripts, so bits per byte is different fraction of bits per character for each script (Section D). The remaining difference is the predictability of the language and of the corpus. 7 Learning to Learn Language PREPRINT Figure 5: Given numerals in context, PFLM learns to count through carries, to order three-digit numerals by magnitude, and to judge approximate sums. Left: exact match of the next numeral while counting from 2 to 99,999, by number of digits, for increments with no carry, one carry, and carry across two or more trailing nines; bands are 95% Wilson intervals. Middle: accuracy at naming the larger of two three-digit numerals, by the ratio of smaller to larger, after in-context examples; at 8192 examples accuracy falls from 0.97 at ratio 1/2 to 0.68 at 14/15. Right: accuracy at judging whether n1 + n2 exceeds n3, by the ratio of the sum to n3; n3 exceeds either addend, so comparing one addend to n3 scores at chance [2]. Chance is one half; 500 queries per ratio bin and shot count, none of them among the examples. Table 2: PFLM compresses real data from every tested domain below an online bigram, gzip, and PPMd. Bits per byte, mean over windows of 524,288 bytes, up to 32 per domain across its categories, against three baselines: an online bigram (first-order statistics), gzip (repetition), and PPMd (high-order adaptive statistics). PFLM is lowest in every row. bigram gzip Domain PFLM PPMd Source code Molecules Protein DNA Symbolic music Audio (µ-law) 3.76 2.36 4.21 1.99 3.59 5.32 2.40 1.47 4.44 2.25 3.93 6.35 1.82 0.95 4.13 2.09 2.99 4. 1.54 0.82 3.89 1.94 2.63 4.18 4.2 Beyond language Number. We test three abilities on numerals in context: counting, magnitude comparison, and approximate addition (Figure 5). Counting upward, the model produces the next numeral exactly by three digits when no carry is needed, one digit later when the increment carries, and two digits later when it carries across trailing nines. Asked which of two three-digit numerals is larger, accuracy at 8192 examples falls from 0.97 when one is half the other to 0.68 when they differ by fifteenth, the distance effect Moyer and Landauer observed in people comparing digits [24]. Asked whether the sum of two numerals exceeds third, accuracy falls the same way, from 0.93 to 0.62, among trios whose sum and third number have the same digit count, so no length cue carries it. similar ratio dependence, the signature of the approximate number sense [7], can be observed in preschool children, who learn to add and compare quantities before they learn to compute exact sums [2, 12]. Deterministic sequences. We condition the model on four binary sequences with known generators (Figure 1b). Each term of RudinShapiro is simple function of the binary digits of its index, yet its correlations vanish at every lag, so no pairwise or low-order statistic predicts it [1]. The cost falls to 0.04 bits per symbol by million digits. The Kolakoski sequence is its own run-length encoding [37]: it has no closed form and no period, and each new term is read off an earlier one. The cost falls to 0.11 by hundred thousand digits and stays near there, 0.13 at million. On the prime indicator the cost settles at 0.28 after one million digits, below the 0.37 paid by predictor that knows only how primes thin out as 1/ ln n. On the binary digits of π the cost stays at one bit throughout: the sequence is computable, but nothing in prefix reveals the rule. 8 Learning to Learn Language PREPRINT Other domains. We test the same weights on six further domains  (Table 2)  : speech as 8-bit µ-law audio [26], piano performances as MIDI events [15], proteins as residue strings [36], source code [31], bacterial genome [3], and molecules as SMILES strings [30]. We compare against three general-purpose compressors: an online bigram, gzip, and PPMd. On every domain PFLM has the lowest bits per byte. The margin over the best compressor is smallest on DNA and largest on audio and music.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Prior-Fitted Networks train transformers on synthetic samples from designed prior [16, 25]. The trained network performs amortized Bayesian inference on real data it has never seen. The recipe extends to domains such as in-context regression of function classes [11], survival analysis [32], and tabular prediction at scale [17]. Whether the recipe extends to in-context learning of natural language had not been tested. In cognitive science, the recipe has been carried to language. McCoy and Griffiths [22] distill Bayesian prior over formal languages into network by meta-learning, giving it the inductive biases for rapid language learning, then train the network on real English. Our prior holds no language, only generic dynamics, and PFLM never sees real text: what it knows of natural language, and of structure beyond it, it infers from context alone. Learning Universal Predictors Grau-Moya et al. [13] meta-trains transformers on sequences from random programs run on universal Turing machines (UTMs), approximating the Solomonoff prior [35]. Grau-Moya et al. is PFLMs closest sibling, with one substitution: UTM prior over arbitrary programs in place of domain-targeted SCM. They ask whether transformers approach Solomonoff in general. We ask whether domain-targeted prior transfers to specific natural domain not seen during training. Language models have been pretrained on synthetic text before. TinyStories [10] produces coherent English from small models trained only on GPT-generated stories using 3-year-olds vocabulary. Textbooks Are All You Need [14] extends the same recipe to code via synthetic textbooks. Earlier work showed that pretraining on structured non-linguistic sequences (MIDI music, Java code, parentheses) transfers to real text via syntactic structure alone [27]. The first two pretrain on synthetic text; the third shows that even non-linguistic structure transfers. PFLMs prior shares neither content nor syntax with text, only its statistics. The BabyLM challenge [38] takes the opposite route, keeping the data real and capping it at childs budget of 10M or 100M words. The cap bounds the corpus, not the exposure: winning entries revisit it for hundreds of epochs, whereas PFLM reads each byte of real text once. In-context learning (ICL) was first demonstrated at scale in GPT-3 [5]: an autoregressive transformer performs new tasks from prompt without weight updates. It emerges only from bursty, heavy-tailed training data, not from i.i.d. data [6], and has been formalized as implicit Bayesian inference over latent task variable [39]. PFLM is clean test case for these accounts: its entire in-context ability comes from prior of known structure, and it is evaluated on domain its training data does not contain.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented PFLM, byte-level transformer trained on no real data, which learns to predict language, numerals, and deterministic sequences it never saw during training. They differ as data but pose the same inference problem: identify the structured source behind prefix and predict its continuation. Trained by next-token prediction on samples from prior over such sources, the model approximates the Bayesian predictor for that problem (Section 2.1). On Wikipedia text in six languages, bits per byte fall steadily as the context grows with the weights fixed. Beyond language, PFLM learns to count through carries, to compare magnitudes, and to add approximately. It predicts RudinShapiro, Kolakoski, and the prime indicator far below chance. The model has not learned language. It has learned to learn one. Context length currently limits how far in-context learning can get. The trained context is one million bytes, about two hundred thousand English words, and at that length the prediction on Wikipedia still falls short of what modern language models reach after training on trillions of tokens. We expect two lines of future work to be the most rewarding: applying the prior to domains with little data, such as low-resource languages, undeciphered scripts, or animal communication, and joint pretraining on real text and prior samples to enhance the in-context learning of conventional language models. 9 Learning to Learn Language PREPRINT

sections.title: B Model and training
sections.content: Table 4 gives the shape of the model of Section 2.4, and Table 5 the optimization. Table 4: Model configuration: blocks of three gated linear-attention layers followed by one sliding-window attention layer, SwiGLU MLPs, and the 256-byte vocabulary. The parameter count is measured. Parameters Layers (linear attn. + SWA) Hidden size MLP intermediate size Attention heads / KV heads Attention head dim Linear-attn. value / key heads Linear-attn. head dim (key, value) Vocabulary 295M 20 (15 + 5) 1024 2048 16 / 8 128 16 / 8 128 256 PFLM is trained in six stages of increasing context length, each stage initialized from the last: 210, 212, 214, 216, 218, and 220 bytes, for 20, 60, 40, 15, 10, and 5 billion tokens respectively, 150 billion in all. Every stage draws its sequences afresh from the prior at that length, so no sequence is seen twice, and the learning rates are set per stage. The gated linear-attention layers run on the FlashQLA kernels [43], built on flash-linear-attention [41]; the sliding-window attention layers use FlashAttention-3 [33]. Byte-frequency profiles Figure 6 places ten random samples from the prior of Section 3 beside the six natural-language corpora. Each natural language pins to the script-specific UTF-8 range its writing system occupies; each prior sample spreads its mass over different region of the byte space, never the same one twice. The two cover the same breadth without sharing script. 13 Learning to Learn Language PREPRINT Hyperparameter Value Table 5: Optimization hyperparameters. sections.title: D Evaluation protocol
sections.content: Every evaluation of Sections 4.1 and 4.2 uses the PFLM checkpoint with frozen weights; the model adapts to corpus only through its context, never through gradient step. Encoding. Each corpus is stream of raw bytes, and the models vocabulary is the 256 byte values throughout (Section 2.4). Natural-language text is encoded with UTF-8; the binary digit sequences map each symbol to one of two byte values. byte on every context axis is thus one encoded byte, and bits per byte (BPB) is measured per byte 14 Learning to Learn Language PREPRINT rather than per character. This matters most for the multilingual panel of Figure 1: under UTF-8 the Latin script of English costs about one byte per character, Arabic about two, and Devanagari, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean about three, so curves level reflects the encoding as well as the language. Natural language. The six languages are English, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Japanese, and Korean, taken from the wikimedia/wikipedia 20231101 Wikipedia dump (one date-prefixed configuration per language). Articles are streamed, concatenated, and cut into fixed-length byte sequences held out from training; the statistical-signature analysis of Section 3 uses 500 sequences of 4096 bytes per language. The acquisition curves of Figure 1 condition on 32 sequences of 1,048,576 bytes per language, each starting at an article boundary, and report the mean cost at every position with the standard error across sequences. Metric and bands. BPB at position is log2 pθ(yt y<t), the models surprisal at the next byte given the prefix. The acquisition curves of Figure 1 plot this against as the prefix grows, with the weights fixed throughout. Uncertainty bands are defined in each figures caption. Digit sequences. The four sequences of Figure 1b are generated deterministically from their definitions: the Rudin Shapiro sequence (parity of the number of pairs of adjacent ones in the binary expansion), the Kolakoski sequence (its own run-length encoding), the prime indicator χ(n) = 1[n prime], and the binary digits of π. Each is over binary alphabet mapped to two byte values, so chance is one bit per symbol. The floor quoted for the prime indicator is the cost of predictor that knows only the density of primes near n, the binary entropy of 1/ ln n, which is 0.37 bits at = 106. Number. Counting reads the stream 2, 3, 4, . . . up to 99,999 as decimal numerals separated by commas and scores each numeral by exact match of the greedy decode given the stream so far; numbers are grouped by digit count and by whether the increment carries. Comparison and approximate addition are few-shot: each trial is example lines followed by query line, scored from the logits at the answer position restricted to the two label bytes. comparison line reads n1, n2=L with = 1 when the second numeral is larger; both numerals have three digits, and query pairs are drawn per ratio bin of the smaller to the larger and never appear among the examples. An approximate-addition line reads n1+n2, n3=L with = 1 when the sum exceeds n3; n3 exceeds either addend alone, and queries are binned by the ratio of the sum to n3. Each cell has 500 queries, at = 128, 1024, and 8192.
